Good Plot / Bad Plot: European Stock Indices, 1991-1998

How the same dataset can lie to you or tell you the truth

Author

Yang An

Published

September 30, 2026

Introduction

This report uses EuStockMarkets, a dataset built into base R containing the daily closing prices of four major European stock indices from 1991 to 1998:

  • DAX (Germany, in Deutsche Marks)
  • SMI (Switzerland, in Swiss Francs)
  • CAC (France, in French Francs)
  • FTSE (United Kingdom, in British Pounds)

The goal of this assignment is to show the same underlying data told two very different ways: first as a deliberately bad, misleading plot, and then as a good, honest plot. Every design choice below is intentional – the bad plot is a checklist of things not to do, and the good plot fixes each one.

Code 
# Convert the ts object into a tidy long-format data frame.
# time() gives decimal years (e.g. 1991.496); date_decimal() turns that
# into a real Date so we can filter and format it normally.
eu_stocks <- as.data.frame(EuStockMarkets) |>
  mutate(date = date_decimal(as.numeric(time(EuStockMarkets))) |> as.Date()) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(DAX, SMI, CAC, FTSE),
               names_to = "market_index",
               values_to = "closing_level") |>
  arrange(market_index, date)

glimpse(eu_stocks)
Rows: 7,440
Columns: 3
$ date          <date> 1991-07-01, 1991-07-02, 1991-07-03, 1991-07-05, 1991-07~
$ market_index  <chr> "CAC", "CAC", "CAC", "CAC", "CAC", "CAC", "CAC", "CAC", ~
$ closing_level <dbl> 1772.8, 1750.5, 1718.0, 1708.1, 1723.1, 1714.3, 1734.5, ~

The Bad Plot

Important

Don’t do this. The plot below answers a real (bad) question a beginner might ask: “which market is bigger?” – by just plotting the raw closing values on top of each other and drawing a dramatic conclusion.

Code 
# Cherry-pick a short, dramatic-looking window instead of the full
# 1991-1998 history (hides the bigger, more representative picture).
bad_data <- eu_stocks |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("1997-08-01"), date <= as.Date("1997-11-30"))

ggplot(bad_data, aes(x = date, y = closing_level, color = market_index)) +
  # Fake "3D drop shadow" chart-junk: a thick, blurry duplicate line
  # underneath that adds visual noise but zero information.
  geom_line(aes(group = market_index), color = "black", alpha = 0.25,
            linewidth = 5) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  # Clashing, non-colorblind-safe neon palette.
  scale_color_manual(values = c(
    DAX = "#FF00FF", SMI = "#39FF14", CAC = "#00F0FF", FTSE = "#FFF200"
  )) +
  # Truncated y-axis: starts near the data minimum instead of zero,
  # which exaggerates how far apart the four lines look.
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(3300, 4900)) +
  labs(
    # All-caps, editorializing, unsupported headline.
    title = "FTSE OBLITERATES EUROPEAN MARKETS!!!",
    x = NULL, y = NULL, color = NULL   # no axis labels, no units
  ) +
  theme(
    # Garish background + heavy neon gridlines: pure chart-junk.
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#CCFF00"),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#FF66CC", linewidth = 1),
    panel.grid.minor = element_line(color = "#FF66CC", linewidth = 0.5),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold", color = "#CC0000",
                               hjust = 0.5),
    # Tiny, hard-to-read axis text.
    axis.text = element_text(size = 6),
    # Legend plopped on top of the data instead of beside it.
    legend.position = c(0.5, 0.85),
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = "black")
  )

Every principle this plot breaks

  1. Truncated y-axis that deletes data, not just distorts it. The axis is fixed to 3300-4900. Over this exact window, CAC actually ranges from 2651-3094 and SMI from 5217-5930 – both entirely outside those limits. That’s why the legend lists four indices but only two lines (DAX and FTSE) are visible: CAC and SMI aren’t small or hidden behind another line, they’ve been clipped out of the plot completely by the axis choice.
  2. Apples-to-oranges units. DAX, SMI, CAC, and FTSE are in four different currencies with four different bases. Plotting their raw levels together and declaring a “winner” is meaningless – FTSE only looks biggest because British pounds and the FTSE’s index base happen to produce larger numbers, not because the UK market performed better.
  3. Cherry-picked time window. Only four months (Aug-Nov 1997) are shown, hand-picked because the lines happen to separate dramatically, instead of the full 1991-1998 history.
  4. Misleading, unsupported title. “FTSE OBLITERATES EUROPEAN MARKETS” is an editorial claim the data doesn’t actually support once you account for (1) and (2).
  5. Non-colorblind-safe, clashing color palette. Neon magenta, green, cyan, and yellow are hard to tell apart and inaccessible to colorblind viewers.
  6. No axis labels or units. A reader has no idea whether they’re looking at points, dollars, or percent.
  7. Chart-junk. The blurry “drop shadow” duplicate lines and the neon background/gridlines add visual noise without adding information – they actively distract from the data.
  8. Illegible tiny axis text paired with a legend dropped on top of the data instead of beside it, actively blocking part of the plot.
  9. No data source cited, so none of this could even be checked.

The Good Plot

Code 
# Fix problem #2 first: normalize every index to 100 at its first
# observation. This converts four incompatible currencies into one
# comparable unit -- "percent of starting value" -- so the lines can
# honestly be compared.
good_data <- eu_stocks |>
  group_by(market_index) |>
  mutate(indexed_level = closing_level / first(closing_level) * 100) |>
  ungroup()

# A handful of raw monthly observations, drawn as points on top of the
# line, so the underlying raw data points are visible, not just a
# smoothed summary.
monthly_points <- good_data |>
  mutate(year_month = floor_date(date, "month")) |>
  group_by(market_index, year_month) |>
  slice(1) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(good_data, aes(x = date, y = indexed_level, color = market_index)) +
  # Full 1991-1998 history -- no cherry-picking.
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = monthly_points, size = 1, alpha = 0.6) +
  # Mark the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis, the real story in this period.
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date("1997-10-27"), linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.5) +
  annotate("text", x = as.Date("1997-10-27"), y = 245,
           label = "1997 Asian\nFinancial Crisis", hjust = -0.05,
           size = 3.2, color = "grey30") +
  # Colorblind-safe Okabe-Ito palette, used consistently all course.
  scale_color_manual(values = c(
    DAX = "#0072B2", SMI = "#D55E00", CAC = "#009E73", FTSE = "#CC79A7"
  )) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(
    title = "European Stock Indices Grew Together, With a Shared 1997 Shock",
    subtitle = "Daily closing levels indexed to 100 at the first trading day (1991)",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Index Level (start of period = 100)",
    color = "Market Index",
    caption = "Data: EuStockMarkets (base R), daily closes, 1991-1998"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "grey30"),
    legend.position = "right",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

Why this version works

  • Same base, fair comparison. Every index starts at 100, so a reader can directly compare growth rates across four different currencies – something the bad plot never made possible.
  • The full time series is shown, not a cherry-picked slice, so the 1997 dip is visible in context as a shared shock across all four markets rather than a dramatic isolated event.
  • Colorblind-safe palette (Okabe-Ito) keeps all four lines distinguishable for every reader.
  • Clear labels, units, and a caption mean the plot can stand on its own without the surrounding text.
  • The legend sits beside the plot, never covering data, and the underlying raw daily closes are still what’s plotted (with monthly points layered on top) – nothing here is smoothed or hidden.

Conclusion

Both plots come from exactly the same underlying dataset. The only difference is a handful of design decisions – whether the y-axis is truncated, whether the data is cherry-picked, whether units are made comparable, and whether the color palette and labeling respect the reader. Those decisions are the entire difference between a chart that misleads and a chart that informs.
